title: Leaders Who Dont Suffer Fools Gladly
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article challenges the common assumption that being visibly impatient with underprepared or naive colleagues signals high standards. It argues that dismissive treatment of people leaders privately judge as "fools" creates a chilling effect that makes even capable team members cautious about sharing half-formed ideas. The piece reframes this reputation as a genuine leadership liability rather than a badge of rigor, concluding that leaders who don't suffer fools gladly ultimately learn less from their teams than they realize.
points: Leaders proud of not suffering fools gladly often believe the trait signals high standards and pushes performance.
Dismissive or impatient reactions create a chilling effect that discourages open idea-sharing, even from capable team members.
This behavior erodes trust because team members read it as a sign the leader doesn't care about their feelings.
The reputation ultimately costs leaders valuable insight into what their team actually thinks.
The article reframes impatience with others as a leadership weakness rather than a virtue.
quotes: Leaders who don’t suffer fools gladly, as the expression goes, have a difficult time tolerating incompetence or sloppy thinking.
While this reputation has some advantages, it is generally not the compliment leaders secretly think it is.

When leaders treat people dismissively, for the perception of adding too little to the discussion, they create a chilling effect on everyone’s willingness to take conversational risks and express ideas openly.
They rightly believe a leader who lets it be known through their actions and comments that they perceive a fool in their midst likely doesn’t care about people’s feelings.
As it turns out, leaders who don’t suffer fools gladly look profoundly foolish in the eyes of others.
